title: Two-step sign-in and a password manager: set up in ten minutes
performance: at their own work account, the viewer can turn on two-step sign-in with an authenticator app, save its backup codes, save and generate a unique password in a password manager, and follow the four lost-phone steps

audience.assumed_prior: signs in with passwords every day and uses a smartphone; has never set up an authenticator app or a password manager
audience.why: the brief's audience: corporate employees of any department, not IT staff
audience.motivation: does not want to be the account that gets broken into or locked out; mild impatience with security chores
audience.context: work laptop, sound on, may follow along with the phone in hand

strategy.name: worked_example_led
strategy.rationale: a software procedure is learned by watching it done once, click by click, on one running case, then naming why each step matters
strategy.signature_move: show the click on screen while naming it, then say in one line what that step protects

misconceptions.belief: a strong password is enough on its own
misconceptions.why_tempting: strength is what password rules have always asked for

misconceptions.belief: two-step sign-in makes an account unhackable
misconceptions.why_tempting: it feels like a second lock that cannot be picked

misconceptions.belief: if I lose my phone I am locked out for good
misconceptions.why_tempting: the codes live on the phone

hook.sketch: Sam's password from an old shopping site leaks; the same password opens Sam's work account. A password alone was one lock someone else could copy.

arc.promise: two settings, a few minutes, and a leaked password stops being enough
arc.bridge_from_prior: sec1 starts from the sign-in page the viewer already uses every morning

sections.goal: the viewer can explain why a password alone fails and what a second step adds
concepts: something you know plus something you have
sections.carrier: before and after on the sign-in page

sections.goal: the viewer can use an authenticator app to turn on two-step sign-in and save the backup codes
sections.carrier: screencast walkthrough: laptop screen with the phone beside it

sections.goal: the viewer can use a password manager to save a login and generate a unique password
sections.carrier: screencast walkthrough of a generic password manager

sections.goal: the viewer can apply the lost-phone steps in order to get back in safely

arc.payoff: back to Sam: the same leaked password is typed by someone else and stops at the code screen

practice_ladder.what: the lost-phone path: the viewer is asked for the first step before it appears
the viewer sets it up on their own work account today

recall_moments.prompt_sketch: Where do your backup codes go? Not only on the phone.
Your phone is gone. What is the first thing you do to get back in?
recall_moments.answer: sign in with a backup code, then tell IT
recall_moments.tempting_wrong: turning two-step sign-in off: that removes the protection instead of moving it to the new phone

transfer_tasks: turn on two-step sign-in on your work account today and store the backup codes the way IT says
replace one reused password with a generated one this week

persona.voice: a calm colleague at the next desk, showing you on their own screen
persona.delivery_notes: steady and unhurried on clicks, slower on the QR scan and backup codes, brisk on the recap

gagne.attention: hook: Sam's leaked password opens the work account
gagne.objective: promise: a leaked password stops being enough
gagne.recall_prior: sec1 starts from the familiar sign-in page
gagne.present: sections in the order you would do them
gagne.guidance: signature move: click, then what it protects
gagne.practice: recall prompt after sec2, quiz after sec4
gagne.feedback: quiz answer explained with the tempting wrong move
gagne.transfer: set it up today on your own account

merrill.problem_centered: Sam's account is the running problem
merrill.demonstration: click-by-click walkthroughs in sec2 and sec3
merrill.application: faded lost-phone path and the quiz

mayer.coherence: one person, one set of screens; no side stories
mayer.signalling: the clicked control highlighted as it is named
mayer.redundancy: screens show the interface and labels only; narration explains
mayer.contiguity: each click happens as it is spoken
mayer.segmenting: four short sections, one task each
mayer.pre_training: sec1 names the second factor before the setup shows it

arcs.confidence: every click shown before anything is asked
arcs.satisfaction: the payoff: the attacker stops at the code screen
